candidate_passage: Two notices disagreed about when the bridge would close. The council notice was dated that morning and named the affected street. A community post repeated an older warning but did not link to its source. Students compared the details with the current map before deciding which notice deserved more confidence.

weekly_context.conceptual_spine: Judge a source using authorship, evidence, purpose and consistency.

candidate_passage: The two notices appeared convincing for different reasons. One came from the council and included the morning's date, but its map had not yet been updated. The community post linked to a map that showed the closure correctly, although the post itself was unsigned. The class had to weigh authorship against consistency rather than relying on a single clue.

weekly_context.conceptual_spine: Judge a source using authorship, evidence, purpose and consistency.

candidate_passage: Authority alone did not settle the disagreement. The council notice carried a current timestamp and named the responsible department, yet one location detail conflicted with the latest map. The community account lacked formal attribution but accurately reproduced two details later confirmed elsewhere. Students therefore had to distinguish authority from corroboration.

weekly_context.conceptual_spine: Judge a source using authorship, evidence, purpose and consistency.

candidate_passage: Although the council bulletin carried the strongest institutional authority, its credibility was complicated by a location detail that lagged behind the updated map. The community account, by contrast, offered no transparent attribution; nevertheless, two of its claims were independently consistent with later information. Neither cue was sufficient on its own. A defensible judgement required separating authority from corroboration and considering whether an error weakened the whole source or only one claim.
